title: I'm shipping a bullet hell game on Steam using AI. Here's what nobody tells you about the gap between prototype and production.
author: Crunchfest3
selftext:
A few months ago I released the demo for **Codex Mortis**, a necromancy-themed survivor/bullet hell, on Steam. It runs on a custom ECS engine in TypeScript + PixiJS + bitECS and was built almost entirely through AI-assisted development. Today it's live at Steam Fest, and Early Access launches March 19.

The first playable prototype took one prompt. Getting to production took two complete rewrites. That gap between "it works" and "it ships" is what I want to talk about.

**The one-prompt trap**

It started with: *"Make me a Vampire Survivors-style game."* I had a working prototype in minutes. Within hours of iterating I had sprites, abilities, synergies, companions. It validated my game idea in hours instead of weeks.

This is **vibe coding**. You describe what you want, AI builds it, you iterate fast. It's incredible for prototypes. But here's what nobody warns you about: vibe coding builds debt faster than it builds features.

After a few weeks of "add X," performance tanked, files grew to thousands of lines, and every new feature needed hacks on top of hacks. So I refactored. Proper game loop, separated rendering from physics. Then I tried 16x more enemies on screen and that broke everything again.

So I threw it all away and started over with a new stack, proper ECS, and batched rendering. This happened twice. And honestly it wasn't painful, because AI makes rewrites cheap. When rewriting takes hours instead of weeks, code stops being "your baby" and becomes a tool you swap out when it breaks.

**Vibe coding vs. vibe engineering**

**Vibe coding** is "make me X." You get fast results but zero architectural coherence.

**Vibe engineering** is "build system X using module Y, following pattern Z, respecting constraint W." You're still working verbally, but you're feeding AI architectural context about how systems connect, what already exists, and what constraints matter.

The shift is from just telling AI **what** you want to telling it **what you want and how it fits into everything else**. This matters because AI is a great programmer but a terrible architect. It writes excellent code to spec but it won't see the big picture, predict future needs, or maintain consistency unless you explicitly tell it to. Your prompts are your architecture.

**The role shift nobody talks about**

I have 10 years in gamedev as a solo dev, programmer, lead, and producer. I assumed my deep technical skills would be the main asset when working with AI. They weren't.

What mattered far more was my experience as a lead and coordinator. Working with AI in production means defining specs, reviewing output, catching architectural drift, running parallel workstreams, and making priority calls. That's not senior dev work, that's lead work.

On a good day I'd catch three bugs, spin up three Claude Code terminals in parallel, feed each one a problem with proper context, and ship three fixes simultaneously. The bottleneck was never writing code. It was managing the process. My role shifted from someone who writes code line by line to someone who defines what gets built and checks whether it actually makes sense.

If you're a lead or producer wondering whether AI makes your skills obsolete, it's the opposite. You're already trained for the job that AI development actually requires.

**I shipped a TypeScript game and I still don't know TypeScript**

Before Codex Mortis my TypeScript experience was zero. I'm a Unity/Unreal guy. Yet I built a production game with a custom engine in a language I'd never touched.

AI let me transfer universal knowledge about how engines work, ECS architecture, production pipelines, and how things break at scale into a completely unfamiliar environment. I never actually learned TypeScript. I knew what to build, and AI handled the how. The patterns and instincts came from me. The syntax came from AI.

This is the most underrated thing about AI-assisted dev: your domain expertise becomes portable. Ten years of gamedev knowledge didn't stay locked in C# or Blueprints. It became something I could deploy anywhere.

**What this means for you**

**Start with vibe coding.** Prototype fast. Validate if your idea is actually fun before you invest real time.

**Know when to stop.** When adding features requires more hacking than building, rewrite. AI makes it cheap enough that you shouldn't be afraid of starting over.

**Transition to vibe engineering for production.** Describe architecture, not just features. Give AI the context it needs to write code that fits into your system.

**Stay the architect.** AI executes. You decide what gets built, how it connects, and when to tear it down and start fresh.

**Codex Mortis Demo is** [live at Steam Fest right now](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4084120/CODEX_MORTIS/) **and hits Early Access on March 19.** It started with one prompt and took two rewrites to get right. That's the real story of AI game development, and it's a lot less glamorous than "I typed one sentence and got a game."

replies.body: Any thoughts on how I can make sure it's well architected, if I don't understand code architecture?

replies.author: Crunchfest3
replies.body:
I'll ask GROLAF for tips later, but CRUNCHFEST from this site -I have a little programming background, and I've currently built one SaaS from scratch for which I have a queue of customers, so here's some advice from a more non-expert: I think the second instance of Claude Code can only be used to check the correctness and consistency of commits and architecture. You can also use Claude's research mode at the beginning to examine the architecture and create an .md file that will be the parent file for each session. It's also a good idea to prepare a tutorial based on Research mode to better understand it. 

Important thing: we mainly work on Claude Code, MAX package, with Opus 4.6 with extended thinking. It's a different AI programming power than the rest of the market, but it costs $200/month.

comments.author: NoodlesGluteus
comments.body: So did you know what ecs library to use or did the AI suggest it? How specific are you with prompts, for example is "make an enemy using the ecs library" enough for it to start or do you need to be more granular and tell it which components and systems to make?

replies.author: Crunchfest3
replies.body:
On choosing the stack — I didn't come in with a plan. My first attempt was actually in Godot, and it was rough — AI struggled with it, progress was painfully slow. So I asked Claude Code a simple question: "What language do you know best?" The answer was JavaScript + Canvas2D. That became my first prototype.



Later, when I hit performance limits and needed proper architecture, Claude suggested the upgrade path: TypeScript, PixiJS for batched rendering, and bitECS for entity management. So the entire tech stack was essentially AI-recommended — I just validated whether the suggestions made sense based on my experience with engines.



On prompt specificity — it evolved over time, and that's actually the key insight.



Early on, Claude had zero understanding of ECS patterns. I had to be extremely granular: "Create an ECS system for rendering. You'll need an entity with a Position component and a Sprite component. Create a query that filters entities with both, iterate over results, render each sprite at its position." Step by step, component by component.



But here's what changed: as the codebase grew, Claude started reading my existing code and recognizing the patterns I'd established. By the time I had dozens of systems built a certain way, adding system #51 required way less hand-holding — Claude would just follow the conventions already in the project. My involvement dropped significantly once there was enough context in the codebase itself.



I also maintain a [claude.md](http://claude.md) file with instructions — architectural patterns, practices, conventions. Think of it as a style guide for the AI.



It actually reinforces something from the article: AI is a pattern-repeating machine. Once you've "written 100 pages" in a specific way, page 101 comes out the same — because it has context. The hard part is writing those first pages well enough that the pattern is worth repeating.

replies.author: NoodlesGluteus
replies.body: Yeah, I agree with the key takeaway there. AI is great within an existing structure. In a fresh one it has too much to choose from and can end up picking conflicting patterns.

comments.author: poponis
comments.body: What did you use for the sprites? Did you use the AI sprites in the production version?

replies.author: Crunchfest3
replies.body:
**Yes, all sprites in the production version are AI-generated.** But it took a few iterations to find the right approach, and I ended up using different tools for different strengths.

**ChatGPT** was the most communicative and creative — best for concepts and concept art. When I needed to brainstorm what a character or enemy *should look like*, GPT gave me the most interesting ideas. **Nano Banana (Gemini)** produced the best actual pixel art quality-wise, but sprites tended to look too similar to each other. Some sprites also went through **PixelLab's** image-to-pixel-art mode for cleanup and conversion.

**The workflow for enemies is where it got interesting.** I tried the obvious approach first — write a list of enemies, prepare a prompt for each, generate one by one. It was slow, not very diverse, and limited by my own imagination.

What worked way better was a brainstorm approach: I'd just describe the *vibe* of a level — something like "Bone Cathedral, biomechanical atmosphere" — and ask for a 2x2 spritesheet of unique, memorable enemies. Then I'd generate a bunch of these sheets and pick the best ones. The AI's "hallucinations" actually became a feature here — given a loose brief, it came up with things I never would have imagined. For that Bone Cathedral level, it interpreted "bone cathedral" literally and gave me walking pipe organs, cherubins, servo-skulls — almost a Warhammer 40k vibe. I loved it.

The 2x2 size turned out to be the sweet spot. I tested 8x8 (64 enemies per sheet) and 4x4 — the more sprites you cram in, the less attention the AI gives each one. At 2x2, each enemy got enough "context budget" to have a distinct silhouette, color scheme, and character.

**For bosses I flipped the approach** — very detailed, controlled prompts with exact design specs. A boss is a key moment, it has to be exactly what I envision. Regular enemies can be happy surprises. Bosses can't.

The general lesson: **less detail in prompts = more creative freedom for the AI = more surprising results.** That's great for brainstorming quantity. But when you need precision, you go the opposite way and lock everything down.
